Real Hope, Real Change — for the common good. I strongly support a joined-up climate platform that tackles the cost-of-living crisis while building fairer, greener communities. We must urgently accelerate the roll-out of renewable energy — more offshore and onshore wind and community solar — so cheap, clean power is owned in the public interest, not harvested for private profit. That goes hand-in-hand with banning new oil, gas and coal licences: we cannot allow fossil fuel corporations to keep extracting the problem that is making bills and temperatures rise.

To speed the switch, I strongly support banning the sale of new petrol cars by 2030 and ensuring all new homes come with non-fossil heating, rooftop solar and high levels of insulation. Warm, efficient homes and electric transport cut bills, create local jobs, and slash emissions. A carbon fee-and-dividend is a fair way to make polluters pay: impose a carbon tax on fossil fuel sales and return the revenues to the public, protecting low-income households while incentivising cleaner choices.

Finally, we must admit our shared responsibility — I strongly support compensating people in other countries impacted by climate change, because climate justice is part of building a secure future for everyone. This is practical, fair, and hopeful politics: public ownership, true accountability, and a green transition that works for people, not profit.

I strongly oppose this whole package of climate policies. It’s not serious government, it’s the Green Blob’s ideological hobby dressed up as a masterplan — and it’ll hit ordinary people hardest.

First, accelerating offshore and onshore wind and banning new oil and gas licences at the same time is economic sabotage. We’re told to cheer while our own energy security is hollowed out and bills rocket. Then banning petrol cars by 2030 and forcing every new home to have non‑fossil heating, rooftop solar and super‑insulation turns homeowners and tradespeople into unpaid project managers for green virtue signalling. Small builders, farmers and families will pay the prices through higher mortgages, retrofitting costs and fewer local jobs.

A carbon tax with a dividend sounds neat, but it’s just another hidden levy that will be stuffed into prices long before any rebate reaches your pocket. And compensating people overseas while British households are squeezed by energy bills? That’s Westminster priorities upside down.

We should put British workers, families and farmers first: scrap these ideological diktats, stop penalising drivers and homeowners, expand sensible North Sea production to lower bills, and remove green levies that punish the poor. Real conservatism is about common sense, not costly crusades. Scrap Net Zero to cut energy bills — restore Britain’s power and prosperity.

Overall I’m broadly positive about the package — I like that it pushes for real emissions cuts and ties in fairness (like revenue return and compensation), but I’m wary about top-down rollouts and the risk of hurting lower-income people or local communities if implementation isn’t handled justly. I slightly support accelerating renewables and banning new fossil licences, but I’d want strong local engagement and just-transition plans for workers and ecosystems. I’m slightly supportive of a 2030 petrol-car sales ban and mandates on low‑carbon new housing (they feel necessary), while feeling mixed about a carbon fee-and-dividend — the dividend side is fair, but I’m unsure it’s enough alone — and I slightly support compensating vulnerable countries, though I’d want clear, effective mechanisms.

I broadly support this package because it tackles the root causes of the climate crisis while aiming to share benefits fairly — the ban on new oil/gas/coal licences, the petrol‑car sales ban by 2030, and a carbon fee‑and‑dividend all especially appeal to me. I’m also in favour of accelerating renewables but worry about siting and wildlife impacts so would only back big build‑outs with strong nature protections and local consent. I somewhat support mandatory green standards for new homes if there are grants or safeguards so they don’t push up costs for renters or make housing less affordable, and I strongly support compensating people in other countries who suffer climate harms.

Real hope, real change — that’s what Britain needs now. I strongly support a joined-up plan that accelerates renewable energy, stops new fossil fuel extraction, ends sales of new petrol cars by 2030, and builds warm, efficient homes powered without gas. We must ramp up offshore and onshore wind and rooftop solar so communities own the clean power that lowers bills and creates good local jobs. That means banning new oil, gas and coal licences — those profits have heated boardrooms, not our homes — and a clear endpoint for petrol cars so people can travel cleaner and cheaper.

New homes should be future-proof: mandatory non‑fossil heating, rooftop solar and high insulation so families are warm, healthier and spend less on energy. To make polluters pay, I back a carbon fee-and-dividend that puts revenue back into pockets, easing the cost‑of‑living squeeze while accelerating the green transition. And we must act with solidarity — compensate people in other countries already bearing the worst impacts of climate change; justice beyond our borders is part of a fairer future.

This package is about one thing: putting people and planet first, not corporate profit. Fairer, greener communities, a secure future for everyone — that’s the positive, practical change we can and must choose.

I oppose this whole package of Net Zero policies — and not because I’m anti-environment, but because it’s an out-of-touch, costly ideology being forced on ordinary people while elites pat themselves on the back. Accelerating offshore and onshore wind sounds green until you see turbines blotting our countryside, wrecking farm incomes and hiking bills to pay for subsidies. Banning new oil and gas licences while we still import energy is madness — it hands control to foreign suppliers and drives up prices for families and businesses already struggling.

Forcing the ban on petrol cars by 2030 and mandating electric-only new homes with rooftop solar, exotic heating systems and fancy insulation isn’t “progress” — it’s an expensive hit on working people. Many can’t afford electric cars, and small builders and rural households will be crushed by upfront costs and unreliable infrastructure. A carbon tax dressed up as “dividend” won’t fool anyone — it raises costs across the board and invites more red tape, even if a token payment is returned. And sending British cash abroad to “compensate” other countries? That’s virtue-signalling at taxpayers’ expense.

We need common-sense energy policy: stop ideological bans, back our North Sea, remove green levies from bills, and invest in practical, affordable solutions that protect jobs, farmers and families. Scrap Net Zero to cut energy bills and restore Britain’s prosperity.

Overall I’m broadly supportive of this package because the pieces fit together — more renewables, ending new licences and greener homes feel coherent — though my backing is cautious because I want clear just‑transition and affordability measures. I particularly like the public/community framing around renewables and the homes mandate (it cuts bills long‑term), but I’m wary that big infrastructure rollouts and bans could hurt local ecosystems or lower‑income people unless there’s genuine local consent, strong worker support, and subsidies for those who can’t afford the upfront costs. 

- Accelerate renewables (offshore/onshore wind, community solar): Slightly support — I want cleaner power and community benefits, but only if projects genuinely involve local people and protect nature.  
- Ban new oil/gas/coal licences: Slightly support — phasing out new extraction makes sense, provided there are robust, funded just‑transition plans for affected workers and regions.  
- Ban sale of new petrol cars by 2030: Slightly support — it would speed decarbonisation, but must be paired with affordable EV access, charging infrastructure and support for lower‑income households.  
- Mandate green features on all new housing: Slightly support — energy‑efficient, non‑fossil homes are sensible and reduce bills, though mandates should be designed so they don’t unduly raise housing costs and should include subsidies for affordable housing.  
- Carbon fee-and-dividend: Neutral / slightly mixed — I like returning revenues to the public for fairness, but I’m unsure a market tax alone will drive the deep systemic change needed and worry about loopholes for big polluters.  
- Compensate people in other countries impacted by climate change: Slightly support — it’s fair and necessary in principle, but I’d need clear governance, transparency and evidence that funds actually reach and help affected communities.
